name: Zane Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Zane. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a new-build estate on the edge of town, Brookfield Meadows, a big housebuilder's site with about two hundred houses going up. I do second fix, so once the plasterers are out I'm hanging doors, fitting skirting and architrave, boxing in pipes. A good day is six doors hung and none of them sticking. A bad day is the site manager walking round with a list of snags and my name next to half of them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years in March. Before that I was eleven years in a warehouse for a big online shop, picking orders. Then in 2021 they put in the robot shelving, the ones that drive the shelves to you, and they needed a third of us. I took the redundancy money and did a carpentry course. So I've already watched robots take a job off me once, which makes this conversation a bit funny.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the finish work, when a door closes with that soft click. What wears me out is the pace. The subcontractor I work for gets paid per house, so there's always someone shouting that we're behind. Priya, my partner, she's a nurse on nights at the hospital, so we're passing the kids between us like a relay baton.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the stuff that actually matters, like pay and housing. I might post it in the group chat with the lads, half as a joke. AI being a flop would be a nice change of subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I wouldn't totally believe it. I believed the warehouse would be fine too, right up until the shelves started moving on their own. So I'd be relieved, but I'd keep one eye open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly carry on. I'd keep working towards my level three, and I'd keep using the chat thing on my phone now and then, like when I needed to work out how to hang a fire door to the regs. I'd keep the savings ticking over, we've got about three months' worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little suspicious, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep one eye open. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: New kit turning up on site. That's how it started at the warehouse: one trial area, roped off, a couple of men in polo shirts with clipboards. If I saw that at Brookfield I'd know the hype story was over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Priya talk about, if this were the news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the rota, honestly. If nothing changes, the big problems are the same as now: her nights, my early starts, the mortgage going up when our fixed rate ends next year.

S0.say: I'd say good, let's talk about what actually matters, like pay and housing. I might post it in the lads' group chat half as a joke.
S0.think: I wouldn't totally believe it, because I thought the warehouse would be fine too. I'd be relieved but keep one eye open.
S0.do: Carries on working towards his level three carpentry qualification and keeps using an AI chat app now and then for technical questions. Keeps about three months of savings ticking over.
S0.feel: Calm, with a little suspicion left over from the warehouse.
S0.quote: I believed the warehouse would be fine too, right up until the shelves started moving on their own.
S0.fieldNote: Zane has already lost a job to automation, and it colours even the calmest picture. He knows what the early signs look like on a workplace floor. His real worries in this picture are ordinary ones: shift patterns and a fixed-rate mortgage ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where you need unions and proper rules, because I've seen what happens without them. At the warehouse, the people who got kept were the ones the manager liked. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, in the pub, on the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay-ish, as long as it's the slow version. Hanging doors in a house that's slightly out of square isn't easy for a machine. But the factory-made door sets, already hung in the frame, those are coming anyway, and they cut my work in half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever the new kit is, once I've seen one of the older lads use it properly. I'm not first in the queue but I'm not last. I'd also join the union, which on our site is tricky because we're all on the subcontractor's books, but I'd do it. And I'd start looking at courses in something like fire door inspection, which needs a person signing it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've been here before, and the slow version still hurts some people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be okay-ish. What's the bit that isn't okay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay. Even if I keep the job, if a door comes pre-hung, the subcontractor pays me less per house. So I'm working the same hours for less. That's what happened to the pickers who stayed: same shift, more targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on site would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, he's my age, does skirting and nothing else. He's quick but he's got one skill. And the young apprentices, because if there's less work, who's training them?

S1.say: I'd say this is exactly where you need unions and proper rules, because I've seen what happens without them. At the warehouse, the people kept on were the ones the manager liked.
S1.think: I think I'd be okay-ish in the slow version, because out-of-square houses are hard for machines. But factory-made door sets would cut my work in half and my pay with it.
S1.do: Learns new site kit once he's seen it used properly and joins a union despite being on a subcontractor's books. Starts looking at courses such as fire door inspection that need a person to sign off.
S1.feel: Uneasy, because he's lived through a slow change before and knows it still hurts some people.
S1.quote: So I'm working the same hours for less. That's what happened to the pickers who stayed: same shift, more targets.
S1.fieldNote: His worry here is less about losing the job and more about being paid less for the same day, drawn straight from the warehouse. He describes himself accurately as middle of the queue for new technology. He's already thinking about sign-off jobs where a person carries responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency help, like they did in the pandemic, wages paid while things settle. And whoever profits from the robots pays for it. I'd say that loud, online too, which I don't normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's the warehouse again but everywhere at once. Last time I had somewhere to run to, carpentry. If the robots can hang doors and nurse patients, where do Priya and I run to? I don't have an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the overpayments we planned on the car and stack everything into savings. I'd cancel the kids' summer camp, about six hundred, which would kill me. I'd push hard at the union to get notice and redundancy terms in writing. And if I lost the work, I'd sign on straight away, no pride about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like a bad dream where you run and the floor keeps moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning instead of five or ten, what's the thing you can't do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retrain. It took me two years last time to be any use with a chisel. Two years of warning is one course and then it's here. There's no time to be a beginner at something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noah and Ellie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noah's thirteen, he'd already know, he's on his phone. I'd tell him we'll be fine because we stick together, which is what my dad told me when the factory shut. I didn't believe my dad either.

S2.say: We need emergency help like in the pandemic, with wages paid while things settle, and whoever profits from the robots pays for it. I'd say it loudly, even online, which I don't usually do.
S2.think: It's the warehouse again but everywhere at once. Last time I could run to carpentry; if robots can hang doors and nurse patients, I don't know where Priya and I would run.
S2.do: Stops car loan overpayments and stacks everything into savings, and cancels the children's 600 summer camp. Pushes the union for written notice and redundancy terms and signs on straight away if the work goes.
S2.feel: Frightened, like running in a dream while the floor keeps moving.
S2.quote: Last time I had somewhere to run to, carpentry. If the robots can hang doors and nurse patients, where do Priya and I run to?
S2.fieldNote: Two years removes the escape route he used last time, which was retraining. His partner's job being exposed too doubles the threat at home. He's open about signing on without shame, consistent with his views on public support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them: retraining money now, not when it's too late. I'd be on at the union and our local politicians. I'd tell the lads to stop thinking it'll skip us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is almost enough. It took me two years to get useful at carpentry, so five years is one more go, maybe. I'd be forty-eight. Not ideal, but I've done it at forty, so I know I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see which way it really goes, then pick something. Probably training as a robot or equipment tech, the people who fix the kit, because someone will need to. I'd ask Priya to look at the same, maybe something in hospital equipment. We'd put any spare into savings, aiming for six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. There's a plan to make, which is better than the floor moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned waiting a year first. Isn't that time you'd want back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But at the warehouse, a lot of the lads jumped into courses that went nowhere, drone piloting and whatnot. I'd rather see what the robots actually need people for, then jump. One good jump, not three bad ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first to pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways on a Friday, and the TV package. And I'd sell my van and use the bus if the course was in town. The van's worth maybe four thousand.

S3.say: We've got five years, so let's use them, with retraining money now and not when it's too late. I'd be on at the union and our local politicians and tell the lads it won't skip us.
S3.think: Five years is almost enough for one more go, since it took me two years to get useful at carpentry. I'd be 48, which isn't ideal, but I've done it at 40.
S3.do: Waits about a year to see what the robots need people for, then trains as an equipment or robot technician. Builds savings towards six months and would sell his van, worth about 4,000, to fund a course.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, because there's time to make a plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather see what the robots actually need people for, then jump. One good jump, not three bad ones.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Zane shifts from fear to a careful plan, which suits his habit of waiting until something is proven. His lesson from the warehouse is to avoid jumping into the wrong course. He thinks of his household as a pair making the move together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty if people actually plan. I'd want every site to have a training fund paid by the firms, and a proper safety net at the end. I'd say that at the union, and I'd vote for whoever promised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years and I'm fifty-three. I could get a whole new trade in by then, and still have some years left in it. But the end is still the end. It just gives me time to be at the front of the queue instead of the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my level three, keep hanging doors for a few years, then around year three or four move into equipment maintenance while there's still demand. I'd keep about a hundred a month going into savings. I'd talk to Noah about not doing a trade that'll vanish by the time he's qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough off that I'd sleep fine, but it'd be there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know when the time was right to move, in the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the subcontractor starts buying kit instead of hiring. Same as the warehouse: first they stop replacing people who leave, then the trial area appears. That's my sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noah about his own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pick something where you're the one checking the machine's work, not the one it replaces. And keep your options open, because his dad didn't, and it cost him.

S4.say: A decade is plenty if people actually plan. I'd want every site to have a training fund paid by the firms and a proper safety net at the end, and I'd vote for whoever promised it.
S4.think: Ten years means I'd be 53, with time to get a whole new trade in and use it. The end is still the end, but I'd be at the front of the queue instead of the back.
S4.do: Finishes his level three, keeps hanging doors for three or four years, then moves into equipment maintenance while demand lasts. Keeps 100 a month going into savings and talks to his son about choosing a lasting trade.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background but sleeping fine.
S4.quote: It just gives me time to be at the front of the queue instead of the back.
S4.fieldNote: For Zane, time is the whole difference: it turns him from a victim of automation into someone who moves early. He has a clear trigger for when to jump, learned from the warehouse. He'd back policy at the ballot box rather than campaign hard himself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Because it's the only one where I can't do what I did last time, which is retrain. What would help is wages paid while you learn, like an apprenticeship for grown-ups, and some say for workers in how it's brought in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like the second time. The first time you think it's bad luck. The second time you start to think the whole thing's built that way. I'd like someone to prove me wrong.

headlineQuote: The first time you think it's bad luck. The second time you start to think the whole thing's built that way.
portrait: Zane Fischer is 43 and three years into second-fix carpentry on a big housing estate, after losing a warehouse job to robot shelving in 2021. His partner works nights as a nurse and they juggle two children and a mortgage whose fixed rate ends soon. He uses AI now and then and adopts new kit once it's proven. Across the pictures he moves from suspicious calm to real fear when AGI is two years off, then to a careful plan to retrain as an equipment technician when there's five or ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it's the only picture where he can't retrain as he did last time.
whatWouldHelp: Wages paid while people learn, like an apprenticeship for adults, and a say for workers in how the technology is brought in.
